name: bluewater-tales-123-132
lines: A masterpiece used to be a test. Fail it, and you worked for someone else for life.
Europe. Five hundred years ago. You cannot just open a shop.
Every trade is run by a guild. And the guild decides who is good enough.
First you are an apprentice. Years of work.
Then a journeyman. Paid by the day. Still working for another man.
To open your own shop, you have to become a master.
And for that, you make one piece. Your very best.
In Nuremberg, a goldsmith had to make a cup, a seal, and a ring set with a stone.
Then you carry it in front of the masters. And they judge it.
Pass, and you can put your own name over a door.
Fail, and you might stay a journeyman for the rest of your life.
That one piece had a name. The master piece.
It was not the best thing you would ever make. It was the proof you were ready.
Every customer is still asking for it. Show me one job that proves it.
So pick your best job. Photograph it properly. And put it first.
Wrigley never planned to sell gum. He gave it away. To sell something else.
Chicago. Eighteen ninety one. William Wrigley Junior arrives with thirty two dollars. He sells soap.
Shops do not want his soap.
So he adds a gift. Buy the soap, get free baking powder.
And something odd happens. People want the baking powder more than the soap.
So he drops the soap. Now he sells baking powder.
And he adds a new gift. Two packs of chewing gum with every can.
And it happens again. People want the gum more than the baking powder.
Twice, his customers showed him what they really wanted.
Most owners would say, no. I sell soap.
Wrigley dropped everything else. And sold gum.
The next year he launched two gums that are still sold today.
He did not find his business by planning. He found it by watching what people reached for.
So look at your own jobs. What do customers keep asking for that you treat as an extra?
That might be the business.
For three hundred years, one business in Japan has let customers use first. And pay later.
Japan. The sixteen hundreds. If you get sick in a mountain village, there is no shop. No doctor.
The town of Toyama makes medicine. But how do you sell it to people that far away?
Their answer still sounds crazy.
A seller walks to your village. With a box of medicine on his back.
He leaves a full box in your house. And he takes no money.
Then he walks away.
Months later, he comes back. He opens the box. He counts what is gone.
You pay only for what you used.
He fills it up again. And walks on to the next house.
They have a name for the rule. Use first. Pay later.
It should have gone broke. Instead, those boxes are still in Japanese homes today.
Because the seller took the risk. So the customer did not have to.
Every buyer is scared of paying and getting nothing.
So what can you do first? A free look. A sample. A clear price before they commit.
In eighteen eighty eight, taking a photo took a cart full of gear. Then one man wrote eight words.
A photographer needed glass plates. Chemicals. A dark tent. And training.
So ordinary people did not take pictures. Ever.
George Eastman builds a small box. He calls it the Kodak.
It comes loaded with film for one hundred pictures.
And here is the clever part. You never open it.
When you finish, you post the whole camera back to his factory.
They develop the film. Print your pictures. Load a new roll. And post it all back.
He is not selling a camera. He is selling not having to learn.
And his slogan says exactly that.
You press the button. We do the rest.
For the first time, ordinary people took their own pictures.
People do not want your process. They want the result, with the hard part gone.
So finish this sentence for your own business. You do this one thing.
We do the rest.
A shaving cream nobody wanted became famous. With six small boards and two hundred dollars.
Minnesota. Nineteen twenty five. The Odell family makes a shaving cream. It is not selling.
The son, Allan, is on the road when he sees a row of signs for a gas station.
Gas. Oil. Restrooms. One after another. And he reads every single one.
He takes the idea to his father. His father asks the advertising men.
They say it will never work.
Allan gets two hundred dollars anyway.
He paints six small boards. One short line on each. And plants them a hundred feet apart beside the road.
A driver reads the first. Then has to read the next. And the next.
The last board always says the name. Burma Shave.
Then the repeat orders came in. The first in the company's history.
The signs stood beside American roads for almost forty years.
He could not afford one big billboard. So he made people want the next line.
You do not need the biggest ad. You need one that people finish.
So stop cramming it all in. Say one thing. Then make them want the next.
The most famous insurance market on earth was started by a man who sold coffee.
London. Sixteen eighty eight. Edward Lloyd runs a coffee house near the river.
His customers are sailors. Ship owners. Merchants.
And they all want the same thing. News. Which ship left? Which ship sank? Which one is late?
A ship is a fortune. One storm, and it is gone.
So Lloyd makes his coffee house the place that knows.
He collects every scrap of shipping news. And shares it with his customers.
If you want to know about a ship, you go to Lloyd's.
So the men who insure ships go there too. And they make their deals at his tables.
Lloyd never sold insurance. He sold coffee.
But a list of shipping news with his name on it is still published today.
And the market that grew at his tables became Lloyd's of London.
He did not have a better product. Coffee is coffee.
He was the most useful man his customers knew.
So be the one in your town who knows. Answer the questions. And they come to you.
Tupperware sat on store shelves, and nobody bought it. Then one woman took it out of the stores.
America. The late nineteen forties. Earl Tupper invents a plastic bowl with a lid that seals.
It is a great product. And it will not sell.
Because in a store, nobody shows you how the lid works.
A single mother named Brownie Wise sees the problem.
She does not sell it in a shop. She sells it in a living room.
She invites the neighbors. Fills a bowl. Seals it.
And tosses it across the room.
Nothing spills. Everybody wants one.
Soon she is selling more than the stores.
So in nineteen fifty one, Tupper does something wild. He pulls his product out of every store.
Home parties only. And he puts her in charge of them.
The product never changed. One thing changed. Somebody showed it working.
Your work does not explain itself either.
So do not describe it. Show it. Before and after. On video. In front of people.
A man with five bricks once filled a museum. Without saying a single word.
New York. The eighteen forties. P T Barnum owns a museum on Broadway. He needs a crowd.
One morning a man asks him for work. Any work.
By Barnum's own account, he hands the man five bricks.
He tells him to lay four of them on the street corners around the museum.
Then walk from brick to brick. And swap the one in his hand for the one on the ground.
And say nothing. To anyone.
The man starts walking. People stop. What is he doing?
Within half an hour, about five hundred people are watching.
Every hour, the man walks into the museum. And a dozen people buy tickets to follow him in.
It runs for days. Until a policeman says the crowd is blocking the street.
Barnum did not shout, come to my museum. He made people ask a question.
And a question pulls harder than any ad.
People walk past signs all day. They cannot walk past a mystery.
So do not open with what you sell. Open with something they need to know the end of.
Before eighteen forty, you did not pay to send a letter. You paid to get one.
Britain. The post costs a fortune. And the bill goes to whoever opens the door.
The price depends on how far it came. And how many pages are inside.
So the postman has to stand at every door. And collect.
A man named Rowland Hill thinks this is backwards.
His idea. One price. Anywhere in the country. One penny.
And the sender pays. Up front.
To show you paid, you stick a small piece of paper on the letter.
In May of eighteen forty, it goes on sale. The Penny Black. The first postage stamp in the world.
It sounded like a way to lose money. One penny? For any distance?
Here is what happened. In one year, letters went from seventy six million to a hundred and sixty nine million.
Nothing about the letter changed. He made the price simple. And the paying easy.
People do not buy what they cannot price in their heads.
If your customer has to ask how much, and then wait three days, you are the old post office.
One clear price. Easy to pay. Start there.
In eighteen fifty six, a sewing machine cost more than most families could find. So one man changed how the world pays.
The Singer sewing machine can do in an hour what takes most of a day by hand.
Every home wants one. Almost no home can pay for one.
Isaac Singer builds the machine. His partner, a lawyer named Edward Clark, fixes the real problem.
He looks at how piano showrooms sell.
And he tries it with sewing machines.
Five dollars down. Take the machine home today.
Then pay a little each month. Until it is yours.
They called it the hire purchase plan.
Sales about tripled in a single year.
By eighteen sixty, Singer was the biggest sewing machine maker in the world.
The machine did not get cheaper that year. It got easier to say yes to.
A lot of customers who say, it's too much, do not mean the price. They mean, all at once.
So ask yourself. Is it your price that stops them? Or how they have to pay it?
Make the yes smaller.
